transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, Doc, I came in because... well, I snapped on a board call the other day. It was just a small question about the facility budget. Which, to be fair, that facility has been an absolute headache since we bought the land back in '98. I remember telling the contractor back then, I said, "Look, if you don't pour the foundation right, the whole thing sinks." He didn't listen, of course. Nobody wants to listen to a guy who dropped out in the eighth grade, even if he's the one signing their paychecks. I had to learn everything the hard way, built the whole business from the dirt up with my own two hands. 

But anyway, they just asked a minor thing about the numbers, and I just completely lost it on them. Yelled right over the phone. And that is just... it really bothered me, because that is not how I run my company. It's not how I treat people. I've always kept a level head, so I don't know what's going on with me.
Have you been feeling unusually irritable, energized, or on edge lately, even outside of that incident on the board call?

On edge? Yeah, I suppose I have been. It’s like... well, if a door shuts hard down the hall, or if that big printer kicks on behind my desk, I jump like something went off again. My heart just starts going, and it takes me a good few minutes to get my hands steady enough to even hold a pen. 

Which is ridiculous, because it’s just a printer. My secretary, Brenda, she’s the one who insisted we lease that giant machine. I told her, I said, "Brenda, it’s just the executive floor, we don’t need a commercial rig." But she’s been with me since '85, back when we were running the whole operation out of a rusted-out double-wide trailer. I remember the heater in that trailer only worked on one side, so we’d have to rotate our chairs every couple of hours just to keep our toes from freezing off. Good times, though. Simpler times. You knew who you were dealing with face-to-face back then, none of this email nonsense where people hide behind a screen and pretend they know how the real world works. 

But anyway, she got the printer because it does double-sided color, which we never even use, and let me tell you, the toner for that thing costs an arm and a leg. I keep telling the accounting boys to audit the office supplies because people just waste money when it's not theirs. A hundred bucks here, a hundred bucks there, it adds up faster than you'd think. But yeah... whenever that machine fires up lately, I practically jump right out of my skin.
Have you had any periods where you felt unusually good, almost high, like you had more energy or needed less sleep?

Unusually good? High? No, Doc, nothing like that. I haven't been feeling good at all lately, let alone high. And as for sleep and energy, well... I've always been an early riser. Four-thirty every morning, rain or shine. You have to be, if you want to get ahead in this world. 

I remember when I was first starting out, I'd sleep maybe four hours a night in the cab of my pickup just to make sure I was the first one at the job site. It was a '78 Chevy, powder blue. Bought it at an auction for five hundred bucks cash. The transmission slipped in second gear, so you had to feather the clutch just right or she'd stall out right in the middle of an intersection. I actually learned how to rebuild a carburetor on that truck. Took the whole thing apart right on my kitchen table. My first wife, Susan, she threw an absolute fit about the grease on the linoleum. We had this awful yellow floral pattern floor in that kitchen, the kind that always peels up at the corners, you know? You couldn't mop it without catching the sponge on the edges. 

But anyway, you do what you have to do to keep the wheels turning when you're starting with nothing. So I'm used to running on empty and working hard, but it's not because I feel fantastic or super energized right now. I just feel... well, like I said, just jumpy. Definitely not feeling unusually good.
Have you been having unwanted or intrusive thoughts, memories, or flashbacks related to a stressful or traumatic event from your past?

Yeah... yeah, I suppose I have. It’s strange. I'll just be in the middle of a phone call, or sitting at my desk looking at the quarterly numbers, and suddenly... the blast, and that fire by the loading area, it just jumps right back into my head. It's exactly like a bad film I didn't ask to see, just playing right there behind my eyes. 

Which is incredibly frustrating, because I was the one who designed that loading area. Back in '04, I told the architects, I said, "Look, we need a reinforced concrete bay for the heavy rigs." They wanted to use this cheaper asphalt mix to save a few bucks, but asphalt gets soft in the summer heat. I remember this one July at our old warehouse, it was so hot you could fry an egg on the hood of a car, and a delivery truck literally sank two inches into the pavement. Took three tow trucks to yank it out of there. The driver was this kid, couldn't have been more than nineteen, wearing shorts and flip-flops. Can you believe that? Driving a commercial flatbed in flip-flops. OSHA would have an absolute field day with that nowadays. I told his dispatcher to never send him to my lot again. 

But anyway, what were we talking about? Oh, right, the memories. Yeah, when I'm trying to look at the spreadsheets, the fire just flashes right back into my mind out of nowhere.
Can you tell me more about what happened during that fire by the loading area? Was there a serious injury, or did anyone experience a life-threatening situation?

The fire? Well... no, nobody got hurt, thank God. It was just... it was close, you know? The blast knocked a few of the guys off their feet, but it was mostly just property damage. The whole side of the bay was charred black. 

Which, honestly, is going to be a nightmare to clean up. I was just looking at the insurance policy the other day, and let me tell you, the premiums we pay are criminal. Absolute highway robbery. I remember when I bought my first commercial policy back in '82. The agent was this guy named Phil, wore these terrible plaid suits and smoked cigars right there in his office. You could barely see across the desk for the smoke. He used to take me out to this little diner on 4th Street—they had the best meatloaf, proper diner food, not this artisan avocado toast nonsense you see everywhere now. Phil would just write the policy on a napkin, basically, and we'd shake on it. Your word actually meant something back then. Now? Now you've got fifty pages of fine print, and the moment you actually need them to pay out for a charred loading dock, they send three different adjusters with clipboards to tell you why it's not covered. 

I told my VP of Operations, I said, "If they try to deny this claim, we're taking our business elsewhere." But honestly, changing insurance carriers is like pulling teeth. You have to fill out endless forms, and half the time the new guys are just as bad as the old guys. It's all a racket, if you ask me. 

But yeah... the fire. No one was seriously injured or anything like that. Just... a really close call.
Have you been avoiding certain places, people, or activities because they remind you of the fire at the loading area?

Well, yeah, I guess I have. I've been keeping completely away from the new building. Haven't set foot near it. Which is a shame because we just put in these beautiful custom mahogany doors on the front entrance. I ordered them special from a guy up in Maine. You know, you just can't get good craftsmanship locally anymore. Everything is mass-produced particle board that falls apart if you look at it wrong. 

I remember when I bought my first house back in the eighties, the front door was solid oak. Must have weighed two hundred pounds. The hinges squeaked like crazy, so I took them off and soaked them in 10W-30 motor oil overnight in an old Folgers coffee can. My neighbor, Frank, thought I was absolutely nuts. Frank was a real character, he used to mow his lawn at six in the morning on a Sunday wearing nothing but a bathrobe and rubber boots. Drove the whole block crazy, but he made a mean potato salad for the block parties, so nobody ever called the cops on him. 

But, uh, where was I? Oh, right, the new building. Yeah, I just can't go over there right now. And it's not just the physical building, either. Even the paperwork for it... the mortgage folder, the safety reports... they're just sitting there on the corner of my desk, completely unopened. I know I need to review them, I'm the boss, but the minute I reach for them, my stomach just drops right out of me. So I just leave them sitting there in a pile.
Are these jumpy feelings and memories only happening when you're thinking about the fire, or do they come up even when you're not thinking about it?

Well, it's... it's not just when I'm thinking about the fire. That's the thing that's really getting to me. I could just be sitting there, minding my own business, reading an email, and if a door shuts hard down the hall, or even if the big copier kicks on behind me, I jump like something went off again. My heart just hammers, and it takes me a good few minutes to get my hands steady enough to type. 

Which is ridiculous, because that copier has been making the exact same noise for five years. We lease it from this outfit across town, and let me tell you, the service contract on that thing is a joke. I had to call them three times last month because the toner cartridge kept jamming. The repair guy they sent out was this young kid, looked like he was about twelve years old, didn't even have a proper tool bag. Just carried a couple of screwdrivers in his back pocket. I remember when I started out, you took pride in your tools. I had this beautiful leather tool belt my grandfather gave me. He was a carpenter, built half the houses on Elm Street back in the day. He used to say a man is only as good as the tools he carries. He had this old wooden level with the glass vials... they just don't make them like that anymore. Now everything is plastic and digital, and it breaks if you look at it wrong. 

But, uh, yeah. The jumpiness. It just happens out of nowhere, even when I'm not thinking about the fire at all. Just a loud noise and I'm practically jumping out of my skin.
Have you noticed yourself feeling negative, upset, or down about yourself or the world since the fire incident?

Negative? Down about myself? No, no, nothing like that. I don't really have time to sit around feeling sorry for myself or thinking the world is out to get me. I've got a business to run. Which reminds me, I still need to finalize the quarterly projections by Friday, and my accountant, Jerry, has been dragging his feet. 

Jerry is a good guy, but he's been distracted lately because he's trying to restore this classic '67 Mustang in his garage. He showed me pictures the other day. Beautiful car, cherry red. I had a buddy in high school, Tommy, who had a '69 Charger. We used to cruise down Main Street on Friday nights. Gas was what, fifty cents a gallon back then? We'd pool our pocket change, fill the tank, and just drive for hours listening to the 8-tracks. Tommy thought he was hot stuff because he installed this custom stereo system himself, but he wired it wrong the first time and almost set the whole dashboard on fire. We laughed about that for years. He ended up moving out to California to work in real estate, haven't talked to him in a decade. 

But anyway, no, I'm not feeling down or negative about the world. Just... jumpy. And avoiding that building. But my outlook on life? That's fine.

We lease it from this outfit across town, and let me tell you, the service contract on that thing is a joke. I had to call them three times last month because the toner cartridge kept jamming. The repair guy they sent out was this young kid, looked like he was about twelve years old, didn't even have a proper tool bag. Just carried a couple of screwdrivers in his back pocket. I remember when I started out, you took pride in your tools. I had this beautiful leather tool belt my grandfather gave me. He was a carpenter, built half the houses on Elm Street back in the day. He used to say a man is only as good as the tools he carries. He had this old wooden level with the glass vials... they just don't make them like that anymore. Now everything is plastic and digital, and it breaks if you look at it wrong. 

But, uh, yeah. The jumpiness. It just happens out of nowhere, even when I'm not thinking about the fire at all. Just a loud noise and I'm practically jumping out of my skin.

inference.note: The patient continues to endorse symptoms of re-experiencing (intrusive memories of the fire), hypervigilance (being jumpy, easily startled by loud noises), and avoidance (of the new building and related paperwork), consistent with PTSD (F43.1). The presence of persistent anxiety, irritability, and sleep disturbance also supports a trauma-related disorder. The continued absence of manic or hypomanic symptoms makes bipolar disorder (F31.0-F31.9) less likely. The symptoms are not better explained by an adjustment disorder alone (F43.2), but both remain possible at this stage.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient is experiencing persistent negative emotional state related to the trauma, which helps differentiate between PTSD and adjustment disorder.
doctor.question: Have you noticed yourself feeling negative, upset, or down about yourself or the world since the fire incident?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about negative beliefs or expectations about oneself or the world, or a persistent negative emotional state. My profile only includes an inability to experience positive emotions (S076), which is a distinct symptom.

patient.answer:
Negative? Down about myself? No, no, nothing like that. I don't really have time to sit around feeling sorry for myself or thinking the world is out to get me. I've got a business to run. Which reminds me, I still need to finalize the quarterly projections by Friday, and my accountant, Jerry, has been dragging his feet. 

Jerry is a good guy, but he's been distracted lately because he's trying to restore this classic '67 Mustang in his garage. He showed me pictures the other day. Beautiful car, cherry red. I had a buddy in high school, Tommy, who had a '69 Charger. We used to cruise down Main Street on Friday nights. Gas was what, fifty cents a gallon back then? We'd pool our pocket change, fill the tank, and just drive for hours listening to the 8-tracks. Tommy thought he was hot stuff because he installed this custom stereo system himself, but he wired it wrong the first time and almost set the whole dashboard on fire. We laughed about that for years. He ended up moving out to California to work in real estate, haven't talked to him in a decade. 

But anyway, no, I'm not feeling down or negative about the world. Just... jumpy. And avoiding that building. But my outlook on life? That's fine.

inference.note: The patient's symptoms of persistent re-experiencing of the traumatic event (fire at the loading area), hypervigilance, exaggerated startle response, and avoidance of reminders of the event align with the diagnostic criteria for PTSD (F43.1). There is no evidence supporting a diagnosis of adjustment disorder (F43.2) as the symptoms are more specific and persistent, rather than a general reaction to stress or life change.
